calls.reason: Ars Technica's account of the FT report backs the paid-tier consideration, and the Washington Post testing (via Futurism) backs the hallucinations. But nothing in the packet shows SGE revenue, cost or profit, and Google already had an ad plan, so the main money point is unsettled.

Carl Brown's review says Devin didn't do the job the client asked for, wrote poor code, and took about six hours against his 36 minutes. Cognition's Walden Yan admitted he changed the prompt and that Devin often makes mistakes.

The only evidence is Cognition's own claim about collaboration and a 2023 study on generating requirements. Neither documents real requirements discussions, and neither shows that AI is generally unable to have them.

The legal hallucination study warns against unsupervised use, and the Chain-of-Verification paper shows errors can be reduced but not removed. Neither settles a sweeping claim that LLMs are 'virtually unsolvable' and unfit for 'any' mission-critical work.

This is framed as Zitron's opinion ('I'd argue'). The complaint shows GPT-4 reproducing Times articles, but its training-volume claims are 'likely' or made 'on information and belief'. OpenAI disputes them, and no court has made findings.

Epoch's projections point to a coming data limit (fully used sometime in 2026–2032), but they are highly uncertain and were revised later. They project a future constraint rather than showing that data was running out in April 2024.
